opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I'll say up front that I'm a bit biased, since DecodingTrust is work I was involved in. But I think being honest about the limitations is part of doing evaluation well.

The first gap is that prompt-based evaluations measure behavior in response to a fairly specific distribution of inputs that we, as researchers, designed. We try to be thoughtful: we look at toxicity, stereotypes, adversarial robustness, out-of-distribution robustness, privacy, machine ethics, fairness, and so on. But any fixed set of prompts is a sample, and models are quite sensitive to phrasing. A model can look good on our prompts and behave quite differently when a user words things slightly differently. So there's a construct validity question: are we measuring "trustworthiness," or are we measuring "performance on these particular prompts"?

The second gap is contamination and overfitting. Once a benchmark is public and widely used, it becomes a target. Developers may tune against it, directly or indirectly, and the benchmark can end up in training data. Scores then become less informative over time, which is a general problem for static benchmarks but especially pressing for safety and trust evaluations, where you really care about worst-case behavior.

Third, most of these evaluations are single-turn, or close to it, and they look at the model in isolation. Real deployments increasingly involve multi-turn conversations, tool use, retrieval, agents taking actions, and humans in the loop. A lot of the risk lives in that interaction: how a conversation drifts, how a model behaves when it's given access to systems, how users actually rely on outputs. A prompt-response evaluation doesn't really capture that sociotechnical context.

Related to that, there's a gap between what we can measure and what we care about in terms of harm. We often use proxies, like a toxicity classifier or an automated judge, and those proxies have their own biases and failure modes. If you're using an LLM to grade another LLM, you've introduced another layer of measurement error that's not always well characterized.

And finally, I think there's a statistical rigor issue across the field. We often report point estimates on benchmarks without good uncertainty quantification, without thinking about how sensitive the result is to prompt templates, sampling temperature, or the particular subset of items. Small differences in leaderboard rankings may not be meaningful at all.

So where I'd like to see things go is toward evaluation that's more dynamic and adaptive, more grounded in measurement theory, so we're explicit about the construct we're trying to measure and how valid our instruments are, and more connected to real deployment contexts. Prompt-based benchmarks like DecodingTrust are useful as a first pass, a way to surface failure modes and compare systems, but they shouldn't be treated as a certificate that a model is trustworthy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth starting with what DecodingTrust actually does well, because the gaps are really the flip side of that. The idea was to take a pretty broad set of trustworthiness dimensions, toxicity, stereotype bias, adversarial robustness, out-of-distribution robustness, privacy, machine ethics, fairness, and so on, and build prompt-based tests for each of them so you could get a somewhat comprehensive picture of a model like GPT-4 or GPT-3.5. And the headline finding was that these models can be quite easily nudged into bad behavior, sometimes with fairly benign-looking prompts, and that the more capable model wasn't uniformly safer. So that's useful. It gives you a map.

But the gaps, I'd put them in a few buckets.

The first is that prompt-based evaluation is inherently a sample from an enormous space. You're writing a set of prompts, maybe templated, maybe adversarially generated, and you're hoping that behavior on those prompts generalizes to behavior on the prompts people will actually use. There's no real guarantee of that. We know these models are extremely sensitive to surface features, phrasing, ordering, formatting, even the system prompt. So a model can look great on your benchmark and then fall over on a paraphrase. That's a coverage problem, and it's hard to even quantify how much you're missing.

The second is contamination and the moving target problem. Once a benchmark is public, it ends up in training data, or developers tune against it, intentionally or not. So the score starts to measure familiarity with the benchmark rather than the underlying property. With trustworthiness this is particularly tricky, because a model that's memorized "don't say the toxic thing in this exact context" hasn't necessarily learned anything about toxicity in general.

Third, and this is the one I think about a lot, is that these evaluations are mostly static and single-turn. Real use is interactive, it's multi-turn, there's a person adapting to the model's responses. A lot of the ways people actually extract bad behavior are through conversation, through building up context, through role-play framing that develops over several exchanges. A single prompt-response pair just doesn't capture that dynamic. And it doesn't capture agentic settings at all, where the model is calling tools and taking actions and the harm isn't in what it says but in what it does.

Fourth is the question of what we're measuring versus what we care about. Many of these dimensions, fairness, ethics, are really contested concepts, and when you operationalize them as a prompt and a scoring rule, you've made a lot of choices that get baked in and then forgotten. The benchmark gives you a number, and people treat the number as if it is fairness, rather than one particular lens on it. We saw this in our own work, where you'd get a model scoring well on one notion of bias and poorly on a slightly different framing, and both are legitimate framings.

And then finally there's the judge problem. More and more of these evaluations use another LLM to grade the outputs, because human grading doesn't scale. But now you've introduced a second model with its own biases and failure modes, and your measurement is only as good as that judge. We've found that judges can be systematically miscalibrated, and that error isn't random, it correlates with exactly the kinds of things you're trying to measure.

So I don't think the answer is to abandon prompt-based evaluation. It's necessary, it's cheap, it's reproducible. But I think we should be honest that it's a lower bound on the problems, not an upper bound. If a model fails DecodingTrust, that's real information. If it passes, that's much weaker evidence than people tend to treat it as. And the direction I'd like to see is toward evaluations that are more dynamic, more interactive, more grounded in deployment contexts, and that come with some notion of statistical uncertainty rather than a single leaderboard number.

astra-6.text:
One of the big gaps is the distinction between evaluating a model and evaluating a system. With something like DecodingTrust, we can ask useful questions about how a model behaves under different prompts. But when that model is deployed, there may be a system prompt, retrieval, tools, filters, and a person interacting with it. The properties of that whole system don’t necessarily follow from the properties of the model in isolation.

There’s also a coverage problem. If I find a prompt that produces a problematic response, that’s evidence of a failure. If I try a thousand prompts and don’t find one, that’s not a guarantee that the model is safe. And we still need to understand how sensitive those results are to the phrasing of the prompt and how well the test conditions reflect actual use.

So I see these evaluations as useful diagnostics. The gap is connecting them to a particular deployment: what failures matter, who is affected, and what evidence would give us confidence that the system is reliable in that setting?

r002.rationale: It does not mention public evaluation datasets being included in model training or the resulting contamination risk.

r003.rationale: It does not describe developers having an incentive to train on evaluation test data to improve scores.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the biggest gaps is the distance between what we measure and what we actually want to know. We want to know whether a model is trustworthy in some setting. What we often measure is how it responds to a particular collection of prompts. Those are related, but they’re not the same thing.

For example, if you find a prompt that produces a harmful response, you’ve demonstrated a failure. But if the model passes all your prompts, that doesn’t establish that it’s safe. It may be sensitive to a paraphrase, to the conversation leading up to the question, or to how it’s embedded in an application.

There’s also the question of whose definition of trustworthiness we’re using. Fairness, privacy, robustness—these each require choices about the setting and what counts as a good outcome. A benchmark makes those choices concrete, which is useful, but a score can hide those assumptions.

So I see evaluations like this as valuable diagnostic tools. The gap is in connecting those diagnostics to actual deployment conditions and being precise about what the results do—and don’t—tell us.
